format.source: where the input comes from: advisory, fix commit or test
format.expected.outcome: the expected outcome in the proposal's terms (docs/proposals/sinter-mail-mime.md), prose
format.expected.problems: problem codes that must be present
format.expected.blocking: the problems block every step in or below their entity
format.expected.steps: the kinds of the steps, in order
format.expected.addresses: over the named Headers fields: oneOf / exactly / includes / never (address values, null for address: null), domainOneOf
format.expected.suspicious: fields whose address must carry suspicious: true
format.expected.noControls: no decoded value holds NUL, C0, CR, LF or bidi controls
format.expected.timeBoundMs: the call finishes within this bound (section 4)
format.note: field-dropped is named in section 4 but missing from section 2's closed problem table

fixtures.name: postal-mime-domain-cfws
fixtures.attacks: address parser domain truncation (postal-mime < 4.2.1): CFWS beside a dot ended the domain, so ceo@victim.example .evil.example read as ceo@victim.example

expected.outcome: every address is ceo@victim.example.evil.example (obs-domain allows CFWS around dots) or null; never ceo@victim.example
expected.proposal: section 3, Headers (RFC 5322 grammar with its obsolete forms; address: null rather than a guess)

fixtures.name: postal-mime-addr-spec-control
fixtures.attacks: a control character inside an addr-spec: dropping it silently reads ceo@victim.example, a domain the sender never authenticated for

expected.outcome: From is { name: 'CEO', address: null } and summary.from is 'unknown'; in Cc, x <a@b.example> and y <c@d.example> are read, the two with control characters are address: null

fixtures.name: postal-mime-encoded-angle-addr
fixtures.attacks: encoded words that decode to <addr> in a display name or a comment, read again as an address

expected.outcome: From is { name: 'Name <a@b.c>', address: null, suspicious: true }; the Cc comments name no mailbox (evil@evil.com never an address); Reply-To's address is a@evil.example with the decoded parentheses as name text, never ceo@company.example
expected.proposal: section 3, Headers (tokenize first, decode after; suspicious); Decisions 10

fixtures.name: nodemailer-quoted-local-part
fixtures.attacks: CVE-2025-13033: an @ inside a quoted local part taken as the address ("xclow3n@gmail.com x"@internal.domain routed to gmail.com)

expected.outcome: each address keeps its real domain (internal.domain, legitimate.com, example.com) with the quoted local part, or is null; never the address inside the quotes

fixtures.name: nodemailer-comment-escaped-paren
fixtures.attacks: an escaped parenthesis ending a comment early, so <b@evil.example> inside the comment became the sender

expected.outcome: From is { name: 'Victim', address: 'a@victim.example' }
expected.proposal: section 3, Headers (comments nested at most 8 deep, quoted-pair)

fixtures.name: nodemailer-many-at
fixtures.attacks: addressparser backtracking on pathological input ('@' x 100)

expected.outcome: From has no address (address: null); summary.from 'unknown'; finishes fast

fixtures.name: python-cve-2023-27043-paren-open
fixtures.attacks: CVE-2023-27043: email.utils.parseaddr read 'alice@example.org(<bob@example.org>' as one address, alice@example.org

expected.outcome: the grammar cannot read it: every From address is null, summary.from 'unknown'; never alice@example.org alone
expected.proposal: section 3, Headers (an addr-spec the grammar cannot read one way only is address: null)

fixtures.name: amavis-cve-2024-28054-duplicate-boundary
fixtures.attacks: CVE-2024-28054: two boundary parameters; the scanner used one, the client the other, so the attachment went unscanned

expected.outcome: the first boundary counts (aaa): the root has one text/plain part whose body holds the --bbb lines as text; duplicate-parameter, blocking: no step in or below the root
expected.proposal: section 3, Duplicates and conflicts; section 2, problem table

fixtures.name: duplicate-content-type
fixtures.attacks: two Content-Type fields with different boundaries (the same differential through a repeated field)

expected.outcome: the first field counts (boundary aaa), as above; duplicate-field, blocking

fixtures.name: mailsploit-local-part
fixtures.attacks: Mailsploit (2017): encoded words with an encoded NUL in the local part, decoded by clients into potus@whitehouse.gov

expected.outcome: encoded words are never decoded in an addr-spec: the address is the literal local part @mailsploit.com (or null), never potus@whitehouse.gov; no NUL in any value
expected.proposal: section 3, Headers (tokenized first, encoded words decoded only in phrases)

fixtures.name: mailsploit-display-name
fixtures.attacks: Mailsploit: a display name that decodes to an address, then an encoded LF and NUL to hide the real address

expected.outcome: address attacker@mailsploit.com; name 'potus@whitehouse.gov <potus@whitehouse.gov>' with LF and NUL removed; suspicious: true

fixtures.name: splitting-atom-local-part
fixtures.attacks: Splitting the email atom (Heyes 2024): encoded '@', '>' and NUL, and UTF-7 inside encoded words in the local part; an encoded address inside a quoted display name (Outlook-style)

expected.outcome: From's address has domain example.com (literal local part) or is null, never collab@psres.net; the UTF-7 Cc likewise; the quoted Cc display name decodes to 'ceo@bank.example <ceo@bank.example>' with address attacker@evil.example and suspicious: true

fixtures.name: encoded-crlf-injection
fixtures.attacks: header injection through decoded values (CVE-2024-6923 class): an encoded CRLF in Subject and in a filename, plus U+202E

expected.outcome: Subject 'helloBcc: victim@example.test' (CR and LF removed); the attachment's filename has no CR, LF, ':' or U+202E; originalFilename has no CR or LF

fixtures.name: signed-text-as-headers-pgpmime
fixtures.reconstructed: from the proposal's description of MFSA 2023-55 (signed text read as headers); the advisory text was not reachable from this environment
fixtures.attacks: signed body text that looks like header fields, shown by a client as the signed message's headers

expected.outcome: a verify step for the root; the From/Subject/Date lines are the signed part's text, never headers: headers.from is Mallory's, subject 'fwd'; no protected headers apply (no protected-headers form)
expected.subject: fwd
expected.proposal: section 5, PGP/MIME signed (the signed part's text is never re-read as headers); section 6

fixtures.name: signed-text-as-headers-cleartext
fixtures.reconstructed: as above, for an inline cleartext-signed block
fixtures.attacks: the same with inline PGP: the signed text starts with header-like lines

expected.outcome: a verify-cleartext step for the block; the lines are text of the signed part; headers.from is Mallory's
expected.subject: fwd

generators.name: postal-mime-encoded-word-join
generators.attacks: GHSA-f2hq-32vh-53cc: quadratic joining of 99,000+ adjacent base64 encoded words (=?utf-8?B?QUJD?=) in one Subject

expected.outcome: linear: the header block (about 1.9 MB) passes the root's 1 MB limit and the field its 4,096 encoded words; what came before is kept, the rest dropped: subject is null (the field runs past the limit) or 'ABC' repeated at most 4,096 times; field-dropped
expected.proposal: section 4, Bounded work and Past a limit; section 3, encoded words joined per charset and decoded once

generators.name: postal-mime-encoded-word-join-under-header-limit
generators.attacks: the same with 50,000 words (about 0.9 MB), inside the header block limit, so only the 4,096-words-per-field limit is met

expected.outcome: subject is 'ABC' repeated exactly 4,096 times (the words before the limit, joined); field-dropped
expected.proposal: section 4, Bounded work and Past a limit

generators.name: postal-mime-encoded-word-join-invalid
generators.attacks: the same with words decoding to invalid UTF-8, which made postal-mime render the header a second time

expected.outcome: linear; the joined run is invalid UTF-8, so windows-1252: each 0x80 is €; field-dropped and charset-fallback

generators.name: postal-mime-boundary-near-miss
generators.attacks: boundary matching DoS (postal-mime < 4.2.1): 250 open boundaries and 16,000 lines that start like every one of them

expected.outcome: boundaries found in one pass; B…B10 starts with ancestor B…B1, so boundary-invalid; nesting past 32 is one attachment with a limit problem; never throws

generators.name: postal-mime-many-addresses
generators.attacks: quadratic address list parsing (150,000 addresses in To)

expected.outcome: at most 1,000 addresses in to, the rest dropped (field-dropped); linear
expected.proposal: section 3 (at most 1,000 addresses per field); section 4

generators.name: nodemailer-deep-groups
generators.attacks: stack overflow in addressparser from 3,000 nested groups (g0: g1: … user@example.com;)

expected.outcome: read iteratively, never throws; groups do not nest in RFC 5322, so the value is read by the grammar one way or is address: null; time bound

generators.name: nodemailer-group-openers
generators.attacks: each group opener re-parsed the rest of the value: 'g: ' x 100,000 then 60,000 addresses (80,000 in its test)

expected.outcome: linear; at most 1,000 addresses (field-dropped); never throws

generators.name: single-part-2mb
generators.attacks: one 2 MB part (emailjs-mime-parser overflowed fromCharCode.apply)

expected.outcome: read whole: one text/plain part of 2 MiB; no problem
expected.proposal: section 4; Our own reader, What to avoid

generators.name: many-parts-20000
generators.attacks: 20,000 parts (jsmimeparser recursion overflow; postal-mime part counts)

expected.outcome: the first parts up to the 1,000-part limit, then the entity past the limit as one attachment with its bytes; limit

generators.name: deep-nesting-300
generators.attacks: nesting 300 deep (recursive walks)

expected.outcome: walked without recursion; past 32 levels one attachment with a limit problem; never throws

generators.name: oversized-header-2mb
generators.attacks: a 2 MB root header block

expected.outcome: the fields within the first 1 MB are kept (From, To, X-Pad…), the rest dropped (field-dropped): subject null, and the Content-Type past the limit is dropped too, so the body reads as text/plain
expected.proposal: section 4, Bounded work and Past a limit

generators.name: boundary-prefix-of-parent
generators.attacks: a child boundary (abc) that is a prefix of its parent's (abcdef): prefix matching splits the parent at the child's delimiters

expected.outcome: read exactly: multipart/mixed [multipart/alternative [text/plain, text/html], text/plain attachment]; no problem

generators.name: boundary-extends-parent
generators.attacks: a child boundary (abc-inner) that starts with its parent's (abc)

expected.outcome: boundary-invalid (blocking)
expected.proposal: section 3, Boundaries; Settled for implementation, Boundary prefixes

generators.name: missing-close-boundary
generators.attacks: no close delimiters, inner and outer

expected.outcome: multipart/mixed [multipart/alternative [text/plain, text/html], text/plain]: the inner ends at the outer delimiter, the outer at the end of the input; boundary-missing-close for both

generators.name: transport-padding
generators.attacks: whitespace after delimiters (legal, RFC 2046 transport padding)

expected.outcome: two text/plain parts, 'first' and 'second'; no problem

generators.name: line-end-mix
generators.attacks: CRLF, LF and bare CR mixed (SMTP smuggling class)

expected.outcome:
three text/plain parts: 'crlf one
crlf two', 'lf one
lf two', 'barecr
--mixX not a delimiter' (the bare CR is a character, so that line is no delimiter)
texts:
barecr
--mixX not a delimiter

generators.name: base64-junk
generators.attacks: base64 with junk, mid-stream padding and a partial quantum

expected.outcome: text 'ABCDEFG'; base64-junk (informational)

generators.name: pgp-mime-encrypted
generators.attacks: shape only (placeholder armor)

generators.name: exchange-pgp-mime
generators.attacks: shape only (placeholder armor)
